title: Investigating the genetic modulation of phenotypic and transcriptomic convergence in bipolar disorder and schizophrenia
text:
Bipolar disorder (BD) and schizophrenia (SCZ) are highly heritable psychiatric disorders, yet much of their
genetic architecture remains poorly understood, particularly in comprehensive populations. Although some
genetic risk factors for BD and SCZ have been identified, the convergence of genetic, transcriptomic and
phenotypic factors across these disorders is largely unexplored. The proposed studies aim to systematically
characterize the genetic, phenotypic, and transcriptional convergence underlying BD and SCZ by integrating
single-cell transcriptomic data, phenotypic assessments from electronic health records (EHRs), and large-scale
genetic data from large-scale and unique populations.

title: HIF2a-VIM-COX4I2 Axis Orchestrates Pericyte Cytoskeletal-Mitochondrial Crosstalk to Drive Pulmonary Vascular Remodeling
text:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a life-threatening disease characterized by excessive
proliferation of cells within lung blood vessels, leading to narrowing of the vessels, increased pressure, and
eventual heart failure. Current treatments only address symptoms by dilating blood vessels, without halting the
progression of the underlying disease. Recent research suggests that pericytes, specialized cells that normally
stabilize capillaries, may play a key role in driving this disease when they transition to muscle-like cells and
contribute to vessel narrowing. However, the mechanisms that trigger this maladaptive transition of pericytes are
poorly understood.
 Our research aims to identify precisely how a molecule named hypoxia-inducible factor 2α (HIF2a) triggers
pericytes to produce more of the protein vimentin. Vimentin changes the cell structure and increases the cells'
energy production through mitochondrial activity protein COX4I2. Vimentin also causes pericytes to transform
into muscle-like cells, driving the abnormal vessel narrowing seen in PAH. To explore this, we will utilize a novel
mouse model, advanced imaging, and molecular biology methods to closely track pericyte behavior and
investigate how Vimentin affects their structure and energy utilization.
 Our findings could significantly enhance our understanding of pericyte biology and lead to the development
of new treatments. By blocking the Vimentin pathway, we might prevent pericytes from transforming into harmful
cells, slowing or even stopping the disease's progression. Ultimately, this research has the potential to enhance
treatment strategies and improve outcomes for patients with PAH.

title: Core 1: Integrated Pathology and Radiology Core (iPRC)
text: The Integrated Pathology Radiology Core (iPRC) of the UW Prostate Cancer SPORE is dedicated to providing expert and reliable pathology and imaging services to enhance translational prostate cancer (PC) research. The theme of this core is to provide our UW Prostate Cancer SPORE investigators with a wide range of integrated and coordinated pathology and radiology services including high quality and extensively annotated biospecimens, state-of-the-art pathology, and advanced radiology imaging. The iPRC will provide services and infrastructure to allow for reliable, reproducible, and high-quality pathology data to be linked with radiologic imaging tumor identification and lesion-to-lesion correlation. This will integrate pathology-radiology data and be linked to comprehensive clinical information as well as tumor-specific bioinformatics. The mission of the iPRC is to provide the type and quality of services that will enable Prostate Cancer SPORE investigators to address pathology, radiology, and quantitative imaging translational aims as well as generate reliable and clinically significant findings that will impact treatment outcomes. Successful accomplishment of many of the translational aims of the Prostate Cancer SPORE projects is dependent on the iPRC services. The specific aims of the iPRC are strategically designed to produce a core service unique from existing cancer center cores that will directly meet the needs of the Prostate Cancer SPORE projects and build a sustainable central organizing force for future translational PC research. The unique infrastructure and resources created to support the UW Prostate Cancer SPORE projects will provide an integrated pathology and radiology database repository to benefit collaborative translational PC research projects at UW and the wider PC research community.

title: Role of TREX1 in age-related hereditary leukoencephalopathy
text:
About 40% of the human genome consists of viral DNA sequences derived from ancient retroviruses, and
functions of these retroviral sequences in vascular dementia are not well understood. The TREX1 protein
regulates these retroelements in our genome, and patients with inherited mutations in TREX1 develop retinal
vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy (RVCL), a vascular dementia that causes disability and
premature death in 100% of affected individuals. We propose to determine how TREX1 mutants regulate
genomic DNA and retroelements to cause this devastating, inherited small vessel disease of the brain.

title: Predator-prey dynamics in a complex animal microbiome
text:
Bacterial predators are predicted to play important top-down structuring roles that can significantly
shape host health. Using a tripartite model system for a complex host microbiome, this project
addresses knowledge gaps in our understanding of predator-prey interaction mechanisms, how
they are shaped by community complexity, and how bacterial predation influences the host.
Results from this work will be used to develop predatory bacteria as an antibiotic-independent
infection therapy with a reduced risk of resistance development.

title: Metabolic control of tRNA-mediated translational reprogramming in glioblastoma
text:
Glioblastoma ranks among the deadliest of all human cancers, with no effective treatment. I will study roles
of a tRNA modification enzyme in maintaining stemness and promoting growth of cancer stem cells in
glioblastoma. This study will inspire the design of potential new treatments for patients afflicted with
glioblastoma.

title: Control of hemoglobin expression by the chromatin remodeler CHD7
text:
Examining the mechanisms controlling red blood cell gene expression and hemoglobin production is essential
to developing new treatments for sickle cell disease and thalassemia. We have identified CHD7, a protein
required for normal development of multiple tissues but never previously studied in red blood cells, as a
regulator of specific hemoglobin genes. In this proposal, we will study how CHD7 achieves gene selectivity and
how CHD7 is itself regulated during development, hoping to identify new ways to manipulate hemoglobin gene
expression and treat red blood cell disorders.

title: Modulatory effects of a retinoid-related protein on intestinal endocrine cells
text:
Diabetes and metabolic diseases are a global and national burden for health care with a high death toll.
Hormones produced by intestinal endocrine cells exert important regulatory actions in metabolism and glucose
homeostasis. The studies proposed by the candidate seek to investigate the modulatory effects of a retinoid-
related protein on intestinal endocrine cell homeostasis and insulinotropic hormone production and will provide
physiological insights that may help harness these cells’ therapeutic potential.

title: Tumor Cell Autonomous and Non-Autonomous Mechanisms of Lipocalin-2 Function in Metastasis
text:
Cancer metastasis is a primary cause of mortality in patients with solid tumors. Our current
understanding of the mechanisms that solid tumor employ to spread and survive within foreign
premetastatic or metastatic niches is very limited, making it very challenging for patients and clinician to
successfully treat metastatic cancers. By defining new signaling and regulatory pathways that control
solid tumor progression, there is great potential to identify new therapeutic strategies for improving
outcomes for patients with advanced stage malignancies.

title: CaMKII: Retinal Ganglion Cell Neuroprotection and Axon Regeneration
text:
Optic nerve damage and retinal ganglion cell loss is common to many eye diseases, including glaucoma and
ischemic optic neuropathies. There are, however, no therapies that specifically promote retinal ganglion cell
survival or axon regeneration in these diseases. A better understanding of the cellular mechanisms that impact
neuroprotection and axonal regeneration may yield better therapeutic regimens, decreasing morbidity and
potentially restoring vision.

title: Regulation of dental pulp stem cell fate
text:
A critical step towards a broader use of mesenchymal stem cells in therapeutic tissue regeneration is to optimize
approaches to maintain stem cell pools that enable healing and replacement of dead terminally differentiated
cells in these new tissues or organs. This project is centered on the study of mechanisms regulating the
generation and maintenance of neurovascular stem cell niches when dental pulp stem cells are used for tissue
regeneration. Optimized approaches that support the function of these specialized stem cell niches will contribute
to improving the long-term outcomes of stem cell-based therapies for tissue regeneration.

title: Understanding the origin of parthenogenesis
text:
PI – Sen Xu
Investigating the genetic basis of parthenogenesis (i.e., reproduction without sex) will provide
insight into the genetic regulation of meiosis that plays a central role in sexual reproduction. Using
cutting-edge genomic technologies, this project examines the evolutionary and genetic
mechanisms responsible for the origin of parthenogenesis in the freshwater microcrustacean
Daphnia. The outcome of this project will lead to novel understanding of animal reproduction.

title: An efficient platform for antibiotic discovery
text:
The goal of this project is to develop an effective platform for discovering new antibiotics. The
platform is based on a combination of two technological innovations – growing previously
uncultured bacteria and screening them for antibiotics by encapsulating single cells of producing
bacteria in microdroplets with reporters.

title: Defining the roles of ZBTB7 paralogs in leukemogenesis
text:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive leukemia commonly diagnosed in older adults, who have a
poorer prognosis compared to younger patients. Many cancers are the result of inactivation of tumor suppressor
genes that keep cell growth in check. This work seeks to understand reactivation of tumor suppressors as a
novel approach to treating AML.

title: Ventral hippocampal circuit regulation of stress-induced fear and anxiety
text:
Project Narrative / Public Health Relevance Statement
Chronic stress contributes to the development of psychiatric conditions, including major depressive disorder
and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), yet the specific neural circuits and molecular mechanisms that
mediate this vulnerability remain poorly understood. This project will investigate how chronic stress alters
gene expression in the hippocampal–prefrontal pathway, and whether these changes contribute to stress-
induced fear and anxiety. This research may identify novel biomarkers and inform the development of
therapeutic strategies for stress-related mental health conditions.

title: University of Washington Medical Scientist Training Program
text: The goal of the UW MSTP is to train a cohort of physician-scientists capable of bridging the gap between basic scientific research and its translation to clinical practice. During their training, students have made important contributions to medical science, helping to improve the health of all people. After graduation, trainees continue to advance medical knowledge and its application, as they assume leadership positions distributed throughout the biomedical research workforce.

title: A Resource Center for Tetrahymena Thermophila
text: Applied Research -Summary / Abstract This proposal seeks continued funding for the Tetrahymena Stock Center to build the research capacity of the community of scientists that use this resource, by designing custom research materials for use in genetic studies. These activities center on two specific aims: 1) Promote future studies with Tetrahymena by developing and displaying new gene expression and mutation datasets on Stock Center informational resources. Our rationale for this approach is two-fold: first, the rapidly decreasing price of DNA sequencing technology makes new data-driven approaches very affordable; and second, recent improvements to Tetrahymena Genome Database (TGD) (such as the upgrade of the genome browser to JBrowse2) make it possible to offer analysis assistance to Stock Center users. Furthermore, because our resources are widely used in undergraduate classrooms to engage students in guided research experiences, we are obligated to offer resources that allow the next generation to train in data sciences. We will identify existing useful gene expression datasets deposited in NCBI databases for curation and visualization on the TGD genome browser. In addition, we will generate RNA-Seq data from key life cycle stages or growth conditions to fill in missing information. We will make these data accessible at TGD and on the WashU epigenome browser, a cutting- edge, genomic data visualization resource. In addition to gene expression data, we will use sequencing technologies to identify genes mutated in a selection of mutant strains with striking phenotypes. This will allow us to improve our resource curation by linking gene to phenotype with the hopes of stimulating new research. 2) Optimize gene knockout strategies for the strain engineering services offered by the Stock Center. As part of our function as a full-service resource center, the Stock Center creates a variety of genetic mutant strains for members of the research community. We will generate standardized workflows with predictable outcomes and time lines for the completion of custom gene knockouts in Tetrahymena. This will allow us to communicate more transparently and effectively with the patrons of this service. Overall, these enhancements to resources and practices will have the key outcome of ensuring that the Tetrahymena Stock Center can meet the research needs of both established and young investigators as they strive to make significant discoveries using ciliates.

title: Mechanistic Investigation of Chronic Neuropathologic Interaction Between Viral Infection and Progression of Lewy Pathology and Dementia
text:
One of the crucial tasks following the COVID-19 pandemic will be addressing the enduring consequences
experienced by the millions of individuals who have recovered from the illness. This project aims to investigate
the underlying causes of enduring olfactory, neurological, and cognitive symptoms that linger for months to years
post-infection, even as systemic inflammation diminishes. We will explore potential interventions for addressing
long COVID through the utilization of an innovative transgenic mouse model and state-of-the-art genetic
techniques.

title: Improving the cancer screening process: Impact of self-sampling tools among underscreened patients
text:
In the US, failures in the cancer screening process contribute to tens of thousands of cancer deaths each year.
We propose a trial to evaluate the impact of evidence-based self-sampling tools on the cancer screening
process (i.e., screening initiation; screening completion; and repeat screening) among patients who are out-of-
date with screening for colorectal cancer and/or cervical cancer. Anticipated study findings, including clinical
and psychosocial data on the entire cancer screening process, will address urgent questions about how to
increase screening and reduce mortality from screen-preventable cancers.

title: Umbilical Mesenchymal Stem Cells: A Novel Window into Metabolic Dysfunction in 47,XXY/Klinefelter syndrome
text:
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) affects approximately 1 in 600 males and is associated with early-onset insulin
resistance, yet the underlying cellular mechanisms remain poorly understood. This project uses umbilical cord–
derived mesenchymal stem cells to examine intrinsic differences in fat and muscle cell development and
function in 47,XXY, independent of postnatal environmental factors. Identifying early cellular drivers of
metabolic dysfunction will inform new strategies to prevent or reduce long-term health complications in
individuals with 47,XXY.
